procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated April 9, 1969 of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Criminal Appeal No. 1055 of 1966.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Punjab and Haryana High Court confirmed the conviction of the accused under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 and the sentence awarded by the Sessions Judge of one year's Rigorous Imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2500, in default six months Rigorous Imprisonment.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The accused appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the sanction given by the Government for prosecution covered the trial of the charge under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

facts: The appellant, a Major in the Military Engineering Service, was charged under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act for allowing another person to cut and take away valuable crops from land entrusted to him.
The government had granted a sanction for his prosecution.
The appellant argued that this sanction was not proper for the specific charge under Section 5(1)(c), contending it was only meant to cover a different charge of bribery.
law: Under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, a public servant commits misconduct if they dishonestly allow any other person to convert property entrusted to them for their own use.
A valid sanction from the government is required before a court can take cognizance of and try an offence under this Act.
application: The Court examined the sanction order and found that the facts detailed within it were sufficient to show that the sanctioning authority had the offence under Section 5(1)(c) in their contemplation when granting the sanction.
The Court pointed out that the sanction order, in fact, specifically mentioned Section 5(1)(c).

The Court dismissed the appellant's argument that the sanction would be invalid because a charge under Section 5(1)(c) might also implicate the persons who cut the crops, stating that even if this were the case, it would not render the sanction against the appellant bad.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's challenge, concluding that there was no validity to the submission that the sanction was improper. The Court held that the sanction given by the government did cover the trial of the charge under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution's case was vitiated by its failure to examine all the witnesses necessary to unfold its story.

facts: The appellant contended that the prosecution's case was flawed because it failed to examine all the witnesses necessary to fully present its story.
The appellant specifically pointed out that certain individuals, such as Gamkhar (Military Estate Officer) and Tehsildar N. L. Handa, were not called as witnesses.
law: The non-examination of some witnesses, without anything more, cannot be treated as a defect in the prosecution's case if there is already other evidence on the record relating to the particular matter about which those unexamined witnesses would have testified.
application: The Court analyzed the appellant's specific claims and found them to be without merit.
For each person the appellant claimed should have been called, the Court found that there was already existing evidence covering the matter they would have spoken about.
For example, the Court noted it was unnecessary to call Gamkhar to prove a receipt because he was not present and did not sign it; the person who did sign it was examined as a witness.

Similarly, since the prosecution had already presented evidence from other witnesses to establish key facts (like the existence of standing crops), the failure to call other potential witnesses on the same point was not a fatal flaw.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, finding no defect in the prosecution's case. The Court held that since the points that the unexamined witnesses would have testified to were already covered by other evidence presented by the prosecution, their non-examination was not a fatal flaw.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred by relying on evidence for conviction that was not put to the accused during his examination.

facts: The appellant contended that the High Court had erred by relying on certain evidence for his conviction that was not put to him during his examination.
The appellant specifically mentioned that documents like Ex. 8, 10, and 11 were not put to him.
law: The law requires that all circumstances appearing in the evidence against an accused, which form the basis of the conviction, must be put to the accused during their examination (under Section 342) to give them an opportunity to explain.
application: The Supreme Court reviewed the record of the accused's examination conducted by the Special Judge.
The Court found that, contrary to the appellant's claim, the Special Judge did put all the essential circumstances against the accused to him.

The Court noted that the accused was specifically questioned about: the symbolic and actual delivery of possession of the land, the existence of crops on the land when possession was delivered, the evidence of a key witness (Telu Ram), and the contents of a specific letter (Ex. P. 13).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the appellant's contention was factually incorrect. Since all the circumstances that formed the basis of the conviction had been put to the accused during his examination, the Court rejected this argument and found no error on the part of the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient justification to interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt by the Trial Court and the High Court.

facts: The appellant was found guilty by the Trial Court, and this conviction was affirmed by the High Court.
In the appeal to the Supreme Court, the appellant's advocate presented a detailed and lengthy re-examination of the evidence.

The appellant raised several specific challenges to the evidence, arguing that the High Court erred by relying on evidence not put to the accused, that the prosecution failed to produce necessary evidence, and that there was confusion over key facts like dates and the condition of the land.
law: The Supreme Court stated its general principle that it "ordinarily does not reappreciate the evidence with a view to arriving at its own finding as if it was a Court of fact."
The Court does not typically overturn the findings of a High Court that has already evaluated the evidence and affirmed a trial court's conviction.
application: The appellant's arguments were essentially a request for the Supreme Court to re-evaluate the factual evidence, which is a role the Court ordinarily declines to take on.
The Court applied its established principle of not interfering in cases where two lower courts (the Trial Court and the High Court) have come to the same conclusion based on the evidence presented.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court found no justification to interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt. It held that it would not act as a court of fact to reappreciate the evidence that had already been considered by both the Trial Court and the High Court, and therefore, it dismissed the appeal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the sanction given by the Government for prosecution covered the trial of the charge under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act.
appellant_arguments: The facts at the time of sanction only concerned the charge that the appellant allowed crops to be cut for Rs. 2500 and misappropriated the money, not a charge under Section 5(1)(c).
A charge under Section 5(1)(c) would implicate the persons who cut the crops, which was not the intention of the sanctioning authority.
respondent_arguments: The facts which formed the basis of the sanction were sufficient to cover the charge under Section 5(1)(c). (Inferred from the court's reasoning and the respondent's citation of 'Jaswant Singh v. The State of Punjab' in support of their contention).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution's case was vitiated by its failure to examine all the witnesses necessary to unfold its story.
appellant_arguments: The prosecution did not produce the evidence necessary to unfold its story.
The Trial Court and the High Court ignored this lacuna in the prosecution's case.
respondent_arguments: The evidence produced was sufficient to prove the case. (Inferred, as this is the standard counter-argument and the court rejected the appellant's claim).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court erred by relying on evidence for conviction that was not put to the accused during his examination.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was in error for relying on certain evidence for convicting the accused which was not put to him during his examination.
respondent_arguments: The conviction was based on credible evidence and was not vitiated by this alleged procedural error. (Inferred, as the court rejected the appellant's argument and pointed to the appellant's own false statements).

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was sufficient justification to interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt by the Trial Court and the High Court.
appellant_arguments: The lower courts' judgments showed 'utter confusion' regarding key facts, such as the date possession of the land was given, whether a crop was standing, and when work commenced.
The appellant's advocate meticulously detailed contradictions and incongruities in the prosecution's evidence to show the findings were flawed.
respondent_arguments: The Supreme Court should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact from the lower courts, as it does not ordinarily reappreciate evidence. (Inferred from the court's statement of its own standard practice).

cases.case_name: Gokul Chand Dwarkadas Morarka v. The King
cases.principle: If the facts constituting the offence are not shown on the face of the sanction, the prosecution must prove by extraneous evidence that those facts were placed before the sanctioning authority. A sanction given without reference to the facts constituting the offence is invalid.

cases.case_name: Jaswant Singh v. The State of Punjab
cases.principle: A trial for two offences requiring sanction is not wholly void where sanction is granted for one offence and not for the other. The court's jurisdiction is only barred for the specific offence for which sanction was not given.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: For a sanction to be valid, it must be established that it was given in respect of the facts constituting the offence with which the accused is proposed to be charged, and the sanctioning authority must have fully applied its mind to those facts. If the facts do not appear on the face of the sanction, the prosecution must establish by extraneous evidence that those facts were placed before the sanctioning authority.
obiter: It is desirable that the facts should be referred to in the sanction itself.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The sanction for prosecution was valid as the facts presented to the sanctioning authority were sufficient to cover the charge under Section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, and the sanction order itself specifically mentioned this provision. The appellant's own dishonest denial that crops ever existed, despite overwhelming evidence, reinforces the conclusion of his fraudulent motive, leaving no justification for the Supreme Court to interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt by the lower courts.
legal_tests_applied: For a sanction to be valid it must be established that the sanction was given in respect of the facts constituting the offence with which the accused is proposed to be charged. Though it is desirable that the facts should be referred to in the sanction itself, nonetheless if they do not appear on the face of it, the prosecution must establish aliunde by evidence that those facts were placed before the sanctioning authorities.

Under s. 5(1)(c) of the Act a public servant shall be said to have committed the offence of misconduct in his duties if he dishonestly allows any other person to convert to his own use property which is entrusted to the said public servant.
why_appellant_lost: The facts considered by the government for granting sanction—that the appellant was a public servant entrusted with crops, that he abused his position to allow the crops to be cut, and that he obtained a pecuniary advantage—were sufficient to sustain the sanction under Section 5(1)(c).
The sanction order explicitly mentioned Section 5(1)(c), demonstrating that the sanctioning authority had this specific offense in its contemplation.

The appellant's argument that a charge under Section 5(1)(c) would wrongly implicate the crop-cutters was dismissed, with the court stating that even if there was such an implication, 'the sanction could not be held to be bad on that account.'

The court found no merit in the claim that evidence was used against the appellant without being put to him, because his own dishonest denial of the existence of the crops, despite evidence to the contrary, 'reinforces the conclusion that he allowed the crops to be cut away with dishonest or fraudulent motive.'
The appellant failed to provide any justification for the Supreme Court to interfere with the concurrent findings of guilt by the Trial Court and the High Court.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution successfully demonstrated that the facts placed before the sanctioning authority were sufficient to cover the ingredients of the offense under Section 5(1)(c), which is committed when a public servant 'dishonestly allows any other person to convert to his own use property which is entrusted to the said public servant.'
The government's sanction order explicitly named Section 5(1)(c), which directly supported the prosecution's case that the charge was properly sanctioned.

The respondent's position was upheld because the Supreme Court found 'no jusllficalion whatever for interfering with the concurrent findinp of the Trial Court and the High Court that the Appellant is guilty.'
policy_considerations: The court adheres to the principle of not interfering with concurrent findings of fact from lower courts unless there is a compelling justification, thereby showing deference to the trial and appellate courts' assessment of evidence.

A sanction for prosecution will not be invalidated on a technicality (such as the potential implication of third parties) when the core facts constituting the accused's offense were clearly before the sanctioning authority and the relevant statutory provision was explicitly cited in the sanction order.
